chunks: Why MOSFETs are so widely used. The question: Why are MOSFETs used so often?
MOSFETs are everywhere because they are easy to drive, waste little power, and switch fast. The gate is insulated, so once it is charged it needs almost no current to stay on.
When fully on, the transistor acts like a small resistor. And in digital chips, paired N-channel and P-channel devices draw almost no power when idle.
Picture a door held open by a latch instead of by your hand. You give it one push, and then it stays open with no effort.
A BJT (the older bipolar transistor, which needs a steady control current) is more like holding the door open the whole time.
The latch comparison is not perfect, since the MOSFET gate does need a burst of charge each time it switches.
At high voltage the MOSFET's square-law I²R loss overtakes the IGBT's near-fixed drop once current is high enough (here about 8 amps). Below the crossover the MOSFET wins.
At low voltage (30–100 volts), MOSFET R DS(on) is so small that the MOSFET wins at essentially every current. Numbers are illustrative, not from a specific datasheet.
Gate capacitance: the gate acts like a small capacitor, a part that stores charge. It takes current only while charging or discharging. R DS(on) : the on-resistance.
Power lost is I to the 2R . Majority carrier: the main charge carrier. MOSFETs use only one type, so no stored charge slows them down.
CMOS: paired N- and P-channel MOSFETs where one is always off. Switching loss: energy wasted each time a switch changes state.
Carry 10 amps through a MOSFET with 5 milliohms of on-resistance. The power lost is 10 squared times 0. 005 equals 0. 5 watts. A saturated BJT dropping, say, 0.
3 volts at the same current would waste 10 times 0. 3 equals 3 watts. The MOSFET also needs no steady gate current, while a power BJT needs a steady base current.
"Four reasons. The gate is insulated, so it's voltage-driven and draws no current to stay on, which makes it trivial to drive from logic.
When it's on it's just a small resistor, milliohms in modern parts, so conduction loss is low and paralleling works because R DS(on) rises with temperature.
It's a majority-carrier device, so it switches fast without storage time. And for digital, CMOS pairs draw almost no static power and MOSFETs scale down to billions per chip."
